newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade bourse turnover down in week to Dec 21.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade bourse turnover down in week to Dec 21.

text.p: The Belgrade Stock Exchange (BSE) reported on Monday a 19.8 percent fall in its turnover during the week ending December 21, and traders blamed tight liquidity and devaluation fears for the decline.
Total weekly turnover dropped to 25.969 million dinars ($5.05 million) from 32.39 million dinars a week ago. The number of deals rose to 171 from 161, the bourse said.
Traders said due to tight liquidity, scarce funds could not satisfy needs of the market where revolving old borrowing remained a key feature.

Market analysts attributed shortage of funds to highly illiquid banking sector. According to the figures by the Accounting and Payments Operations Office, 115 Yugoslav banks disposed of only 64 million dinars last Friday.
But devaluation fears also reflected in subdued activity.

"Some say dinar will devalue and some expect no changes, but both refrain from any market activity. Those who have courage buy hard currency, and those less courageous stay aside," a trader told Reuters.

Speculation that the dinar would devalue first mounted ahead of November 3 general elections in Yugoslavia. Since then, the government gave strong verbal support to the currency promising to keep the currency unchanged at 3.3 to the German mark and use it as an anchor of its 1997 economic policy.

But the dinar black market rate, hovering over past 11 months mainly at 3.4-3.5 to the German mark, began to dive along with the opposition staging mass street protests accusing the ruling Socialists of alleged election fraud.
Early on Monday, the black market rate stood at 3.8-3.95.
Analysts agreed the slide resulted from an unstable political situation, but could not exclude a possibility of a monetary expansion taking place behind the scenes.

"The central bank says there was no expansion in M1 money supply in the last quarter of the year, and if it did not take place, we'll see the black market rate retreating close to its previous level soon after political issues settle down," said an analyst who asked not to be named.
Economists said a devaluation could help exporters and those who owed large dinar amounts, but effects would be short-lived. They agreed any decision to devalue will be political.
For the week ending December 21, the BSE reported the following details:
* Commercial paper accounted for 145 transactions worth 20.788 million dinars.
* Treasury bills traded 21 times for a volume of 3.085 million dinars.
Interest rates on commercial paper and treasury bills ranged between an annual 44 and 793 percent.
Traders said around 30 percent of all deals were struck at daily interest rates close to 0.5 percent, corresponding to an annual 520 percent.
*The bourse reported no sale in the central bank short-term bonds.
*There were two deals in wheat selling contracts sold for 1.843 million dinars. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
